clues.text: This poem's title adjective first appears in Boccaccio's writing of the 1350s, but no edition put that word in the title until a 1555 Venice printing.
Each of this poem's three parts ends on the same word, 'stelle', meaning 'stars', and the whole poem runs to exactly 100 cantos.
Written in Tuscan rather than Latin, the formal written language of its day, this poem helped make its author's dialect the basis of standard Italian.
Dante's epic takes him through Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, guided first by the Roman poet Virgil and then by Beatrice.

divine-comedy.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia says the earliest known use of 'Divina' is Boccaccio's Trattatello in laude di Dante (written 1351-55) and that Dolce's 1555 Giolito edition was the first to use it in the title; Magdalene College says that before 1555 the work was known simply as the Comedìa. Clue 2 makes plain the answer is the whole three-part poem, not the Inferno. Some earlier Venice title pages called Dante himself 'divino'; the 1555 edition was the first to apply the word to the poem in its title, which is what the clue says.

clues.text: This god's head appeared on early Roman bronze coins with a ship on the reverse, which Macrobius said is why boys tossing coins called out 'heads or ships'.
This Roman god had no known Greek equivalent, yet every Roman prayer and ritual had to call on him first, before any other god.
The doors of this god's shrine in Rome stood open in wartime and were shut only in peace, a rare event that Augustus managed three times.
This two-faced Roman god of doorways and beginnings gives his name to the month of January.

janus.writerNotes: Clue 1 is Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.7.21-22 (cited by both section numbers in different sources). Clue 3: Wikipedia counts the closures after Numa as once after the First Punic War, three times under Augustus and once under Nero; the Chicago page says only 'several times' under Augustus.

clues.text: This brain structure in cattle yielded a frog-skin-lightening hormone that a Yale team isolated in 1958 while hoping to treat skin disorders.
With age this structure collects calcified grains nicknamed 'brain sand', which radiologists sometimes use as landmarks on X-rays.
Descartes called this structure 'the principal seat of the soul', believing it was the only part of the brain that does not come as a pair.
This rice-grain-sized structure deep in the brain, named for its cone-like shape, releases melatonin in the dark to help set your sleep-wake rhythm.

pineal-gland.writerNotes: Clue 1 is Aaron Lerner's team (melatonin); frog-skin lightening by cow pineal extract was known from 1917, so the clue says the hormone lightens frog skin, not that the team discovered that. Clues avoid 'gland', 'pine' and 'body' (the alias 'Pineal body'). Brain sand also forms elsewhere in the brain (choroid plexus), so clue 2 says the structure collects it, not that it is unique to it.

clues.text: Early versions of this device read paper tokens laced with radioactive carbon-14, and their designer said you'd have to eat 136,000 of them to come to any harm.
Antarctica's McMurdo Station got one of these in 1998, and by 2015 it kept a second unit on hand to strip for spare parts.
Sitcom star Reg Varney of 'On the Buses' was the first customer to use Barclays' pioneering one, in Enfield, north London, in June 1967.
You draw money from this device with a four-digit PIN, the length John Shepherd-Barron chose because his wife could only remember four figures.

atm.writerNotes: Who invented the ATM is disputed (James Goodfellow's PIN-and-card work, other 1967 machines), so no clue calls anyone 'the inventor' or calls Enfield the world's first. Clue 2 is pinned to 2015 (Mental Floss); a McMurdo resident's 2022 blog still describes a pair of Wells Fargo units. Clues avoid every alias word: cash, machine, teller, automated, cashpoint, dispenser.

clues.text: This meme comes from a 2013 strip of KC Green's webcomic Gunshow, drawn when he was 25 and adjusting his antidepressant dose.
In July 2016 the Republican Party's official Twitter account posted this meme on the opening day of the Democratic convention, without its creator's permission.
In 2024 this meme's creator and Numskull Games announced an old-school platform video game based on it, subtitled 'Maximum Cope'.
This meme shows a smiling cartoon dog with a coffee mug, sitting calmly at a table as the room around him goes up in flames.

this-is-fine.writerNotes: Every clue opens with or names 'this meme', so it is plain the answer is the meme, not the Gunshow webcomic. Clue 1: Wikipedia says Green was adjusting his antidepressant dosage when he made the strip; GPB (NPR, 2023) says he drew it at 25 while focusing on his mental health. The game was released around May 2026, but the clue only uses the 2024 announcement.

clues.text: This character's story first ran as a serial in an Italian children's magazine in 1881 and ended with him hanged, until reader demand and the editor brought him back.
This character's name may come from a rare Tuscan word for 'pine nut', or be built from the Italian words for 'pine' and 'eye'.
Early in the original book, this character kills the Talking Cricket by accidentally hitting it with a thrown hammer, and the cricket later returns as a ghost.
This wooden puppet, carved by Geppetto, finds that his nose grows longer when he tells a lie.

pinocchio.writerNotes: Sources differ on the serial's start (June or 7 July 1881), so the clue gives only the year. Wikipedia hedges the name's origin ('possibly'), and clue 2 keeps that hedge.

clues.text: This Titan fathered the nymph Calypso of the Odyssey, as well as the Hyades and the seven Pleiades.
In Ovid's telling, Perseus showed this Titan Medusa's head and turned him into a mountain, his beard and hair becoming forests.
While this Titan fetched the golden apples, Heracles took over his burden, then tricked him into taking it back by asking for a moment to get comfortable.
Zeus condemned this Titan to hold up the sky on his shoulders, and the top bone of the spine, which holds up the skull, is named after him.

atlas-titan.writerNotes: Versions of the Heracles trick differ (Wikipedia: rearrange his cloak; Apollodorus via Theoi: put a cushion on his head), so clue 3 says only 'to get comfortable'. Mercator dedicated the book to Atlas in his role as a king of Mauretania.

clues.text: In parts of the American South, this body feature goes by the folk name 'goozle'.
Textbooks say the two cartilage plates that form this feature meet at about 90 degrees in men but about 120 degrees in women.
Surgeons can shrink this feature with a chondrolaryngoplasty, an operation colloquially called a 'tracheal shave'.
This throat bump is traditionally said to be named for a legend, found nowhere in the Bible, that forbidden fruit stuck in the first man's throat.

adams-apple.writerNotes: The 90/120 degree figures are the usual textbook values (Kenhub). Measured studies find smaller angles (about 75 in men, 92-98 in women), so clue 2 says 'Textbooks say'. 'Goozle' is sourced to Wikipedia only. Clue 4 says 'traditionally said' because Wikipedia gives the legend as the usual explanation, alongside Alexander Gode's rival theory of a mistranslated Hebrew phrase.

clues.text: The first of these road devices went up near London's Westminster Bridge in 1868, gas-lit at night, and exploded within a month, badly injuring the policeman working it.
Inventor Garrett Morgan, who once used his own smoke hood to rescue men from a tunnel under Lake Erie, patented a hand-operated version of this in 1923.
In 1973 Japan ordered the green on these to be the bluest shade possible, because that color's official name is 'ao', a word that usually means blue.
In an Irish neighborhood of Syracuse, New York, one of these hangs with green above red, after local boys kept stoning it while the 'British' red was on top.

traffic-light.writerNotes: Installed 9 or 10 December 1868, exploded 2 January 1869 (Wikipedia), so 'within a month' holds. Sources disagree on when the Tipperary Hill light was flipped (1925 or 1928), so clue 4 gives no date. Aliases ban 'signal' and 'stoplight'; no clue uses them.

clues.text: A 2009 Armed Forces Journal article titled 'Let's Do This!' linked this video game character to the American way of advising Iraq's armed forces.
In 2017 the two players behind this character's viral 2005 video released its first take, a dry run, to help raise awareness of net neutrality.
In 2008 Blizzard added an achievement that gives players who kill 50 rookery whelps within 15 seconds this character's surname as a title.
Back from fixing a plate of chicken, this World of Warcraft character charged into a dungeon shouting his own name and got his whole group killed.

leeroy-jenkins.writerNotes: Clue 2 avoids saying the video was 'confirmed staged': Kotaku and Wikipedia report the first take and Vinson's 'obviously satire' quote but stop short of an explicit admission.

clues.text: This novel's author said its revenge theme came from a Paris police archivist's tale of a Nîmes shoemaker whose jealous friends falsely accused him of spying for England.
A Cuban cigar brand created in the 1930s is named after this novel, said to have been a favorite of rollers who had it read aloud at work.
Alexandre Dumas spent 500,000 francs building a château near Paris named after this book, then sold it in 1848 for 31,000 francs when he ran short of money.
In this 1844 novel, the sailor Edmond Dantès escapes from the Château d'If and returns rich, under a new name, to punish the men who had him jailed.

count-of-monte-cristo.writerNotes: Clue 2: Wikipedia says the rollers' fondness for the novel is only alleged, so the clue hedges with 'said to have been'. The brand was created after Alonso Menéndez bought the factory in July 1935, so the clue says 'the 1930s' rather than a year. Clue 3: 500,000 francs is the construction cost Wikipedia gives.

clues.text: This figure from Jewish folklore gave its name to a new computer at Israel's Weizmann Institute in 1965, a name chosen by the Kabbalah scholar Gershom Scholem.
In some versions, the Hebrew word for 'truth' is written on its forehead, and erasing the first letter leaves the word for 'dead'.
clues.how: written, moved from clue 3 after review

clues.text: A 1674 letter told how a Polish rabbi named Elias, thought to be Elijah of Chełm, made one of these to be his servant and do the housework.
Legend says Rabbi Judah Loew of Prague shaped this creature from Vltava river clay and brought it to life to defend the city's Jewish ghetto.

golem.writerNotes: Clue 1: the computer was called 'Golem Aleph'. Sources differ on whether Scholem proposed the name himself (National Library of Israel blog, seen only as a search snippet because the page returned 403) or was asked to name it (Times of Israel blog), so the clue says only that he chose it. The NLI snippet dates his dedication speech to 17 June 1965. Clue 2: Wikipedia quotes Christoph Arnold's 1674 letter about 'Rabbi Eliyahu Baal Shem' in Poland (Elijah of Chełm).

clues.text: These tiny sensory clusters each hold 50 to 150 receptor cells, and the body replaces those cells roughly every 10 days.
The average adult has somewhere between 2,000 and 10,000 of these, and children have more, because people lose them as they age.
A catfish typically has more than 100,000 of these spread all over its body, packed most densely on the whiskers around its mouth.
These little clusters, housed in the bumps called papillae on your tongue, let you detect sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami flavors.

taste-buds.writerNotes: Clues 1 and 2 make plain the answer is many small countable structures, not the tongue. Clue 3: catfish counts vary by source (The Log: more than 100,000, up to 175,000 in large fish; Mental Floss: about 680,000 in the channel catfish), so the clue says only 'more than 100,000'. Clue 1: Cleveland Clinic says the receptor cells, not the whole bud, are replaced about every 10 days; other sources give 10 to 14 days.

clues.text: This household product was first made in 1942 by a team seeking a clear plastic for precision gun sights, and went on sale in 1958 as 'Eastman 910'.
Crime scene investigators warm this product so its fumes react with invisible fingerprint residue, leaving a white coating on the ridges of the print.
On the TV show 'I've Got a Secret', inventor Harry Coover lifted the host, Garry Moore, off the ground using a single drop of it.
This fast-setting cyanoacrylate adhesive is notorious for sticking people's fingers together within seconds.

super-glue.writerNotes: Clue 1: Lemelson-MIT and CBS tie the 1942 find to Coover's team (CBS calls him an Eastman Kodak chemist); Wikipedia's cyanoacrylate page says the original patent was filed in 1947 by B.F. Goodrich, so the clue does not name a company for 1942. Clue 3: sources disagree on the year of the TV appearance (1958 in one, 'the 1950s' in another), so the clue gives none. Krazy Glue is a rival brand of the same cyanoacrylate adhesive, added as an alias because players use the names interchangeably; drop it if that is too loose.

clues.text: Barry Diller's IAC bought this search engine in 2005 for about $1.85 billion and, the next year, dropped the second word of its name.
In 2000 this search engine became the first dot-com with a giant balloon in the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.
In 2009 this search engine's UK site remade its mascot as a CGI character, and kept his image there until 2016.
This late-1990s search engine invited users to type questions in plain English, and its cartoon mascot was named after Bertie Wooster's valet in P. G. Wodehouse's stories.

ask-jeeves.writerNotes: Clue 2: BizBash (21 November 2000) calls it 'the first dot-com with a balloon in the parade'. Clue 1: the deal was announced in March 2005 and closed in July 2005 (Wikipedia). 'Ask.com' is added as an alias because it is the same site under its later name.

clues.text: This novel first ran in a Philadelphia magazine in 1890, after its editor secretly cut about 500 words; an uncensored edition put them back in 2011.
This book was commissioned at an 1889 dinner at London's Langham Hotel, the same meal that produced Arthur Conan Doyle's The Sign of the Four.
In an 1895 libel trial, the barrister Edward Carson read passages from this novel aloud while cross-examining its author.
In this Oscar Wilde novel, a handsome young man stays youthful while his painted portrait, hidden away, grows old and ugly with his sins.

picture-of-dorian-gray.writerNotes: Alias 'Dorian Gray' added because players often call the book that; its words are banned anyway. Drop it if the owner wants only the full title accepted. The 1890 version appeared in Lippincott's Monthly Magazine (Philadelphia); the 2011 edition is Harvard's Belknap Press 'uncensored' edition.

clues.text: This figure of Slavic folklore rides a pig into battle against a 'crocodile' in old Russian woodblock prints, which some scholars read as a jab at Peter the Great.
Russian troops in Ukraine gave this figure's name to the big multi-rotor bomber drones that attack their positions at night.
Keanu Reeves's hitman John Wick is known in the criminal underworld by this figure's name.
This bony-legged witch of Russian fairy tales flies around in a mortar and lives in a hut that stands on chicken legs.

baba-yaga.writerNotes: Clue 1: the prints are late 17th / early 18th century lubki; Dmitry Rovinsky first read them as satire of Peter the Great, whom Old Believers called a 'crocodile'. The reading is an interpretation, so the clue hedges with 'some scholars'.

clues.text: This bone seems to have evolved separately at least three times, in birds, lizards and mammals, yet most marsupials have no bony version of it.
This is the largest bone in the body that grows inside a tendon, and its medical name comes from Latin for a small, shallow dish.
Babies are born with this bone made of soft cartilage, and it only begins to turn into bone at about age three.
Doctors test your reflexes by tapping the tendon just below this small bone at the front of the joint between your thigh and shin.

kneecap.writerNotes: Clue 1: Samuels, Regnault and Hutchinson (PeerJ 2017) say the distribution 'has been interpreted as three occasions of independent evolution (in Aves, Squamata and Mammalia)' and that bony patellae probably evolved 4-6 times within mammals alone; most marsupials have only a non-bony one. Hence 'seems to' and 'at least'.

clues.text: One of these appliances at Carnegie Mellon was wired to the ARPANET in 1982, so anyone on the network could check its contents from a keyboard.
In 1995 U.S. safety regulators counted at least 37 deaths since 1978 from people rocking or tilting these heavy boxes until they toppled.
Hero of Alexandria described a forerunner of this in the first century AD: a coin dropped onto a small pan tipped a lever that let out holy water.
Coins or a card go into this hallway box, and out drops a can of soda or a bag of chips.

vending-machine.writerNotes: Clue 1 avoids calling the Carnegie Mellon Coke machine the 'first' networked one: an internet-history list post recalls a Stanford machine on the ARPANET in the 1970s. Clue 2: CPSC release of 2 November 1995 ('at least 37 deaths and 113 injuries since 1978'). Clue 3: Wikipedia says Hero's device gave out wine or holy water.

clues.text: This kind of symbol, typed from ordinary keyboard characters, had its original pair sold as an NFT in 2021 for $237,500.
Vladimir Nabokov wished for something like this in 1969, telling The New York Times there should be a special typographical sign for a smile.
In 2000 Despair, Inc., a maker of spoof motivational posters, won a U.S. trademark on the frowning version of this for greeting cards and prints.
Scott Fahlman of Carnegie Mellon proposed this in 1982: a colon, a hyphen and a closing parenthesis, read sideways, to mark a post as a joke.

emoticon.writerNotes: Clue 1: the Heritage Auctions lot was Fahlman's original :-) and :-( post, sold in September 2021. Clue 1 and clue 4 both touch Fahlman's 1982 post, but from different angles (the 2021 sale vs the proposal itself).

clues.text: This novel's author modeled her heroine's face on a magazine photo of Evelyn Nesbit, the model whose husband shot the architect Stanford White in 1906.
This novel has been on Japan's national school curriculum since 1952, though its Japanese translator had wanted to call it 'The Girl Gazing Out the Window'.
In 2014 Guinness World Records named a musical of this book, first staged in Charlottetown in 1965, the world's longest-running annual musical theatre production.
This 1908 L. M. Montgomery novel follows a talkative red-haired orphan sent by mistake to a Prince Edward Island farm whose owners wanted a boy.

anne-of-green-gables.writerNotes: Clue 3 is pinned to the 2014 Guinness title because the musical stopped running every year after 2022 (now alternate years). Clue 2: the 1952 title was the editor's idea; the translator's own choice is given as 'The Girl Gazing Out the Window' by annemanuscript.ca (other sites translate it slightly differently).

clues.text: This folklore figure appears in Lady Fanshawe's memoirs, which describe a pale, red-haired woman at her window one night while she stayed with the O'Brien family around 1650.
Some people in Ireland would never pick up a comb lying on the ground, because this figure is said to groom her long hair with one.
This figure's name comes from the Old Irish for 'woman of the fairy mound', after the ancient burial mounds that dot the Irish countryside.
This female spirit of Irish folklore wails outside a family's home to warn that one of them is about to die.

banshee.writerNotes: Clue 1: secondary sources date the Fanshawe sighting to 1642, so the clue says 'the 1640s'. Sources disagree on when her memoirs were first published, so the clue gives no publication date.

clues.text: These marks, which Amelia Earhart reportedly disliked having, made news in 2012 when searchers said a jar found on a Pacific atoll may have held an ointment sold to treat them.
In a 1971 Judy Blume book, a second-grader pays a girl fifty cents for a secret recipe meant to give him these, and it only makes him sick.
The model Twiggy helped make these fashionable in the 1960s by not covering hers with makeup, and in the 2020s TikTok spread a trend of tattooing on fake ones.
These small, flat light-brown spots are common on fair skin, and they darken with time in the sun and fade with less of it.

freckles.writerNotes: Clue 1 is hedged on purpose: TIGHAR said the jar resembles Dr. C. H. Berry's Freckle Ointment but admitted it cannot be tied directly to Earhart.

clues.text: In 1943 Vesta Stoudt, an Illinois munitions worker with two sons in the Navy, wrote to President Roosevelt proposing this household staple as a sturdier seal for ammunition boxes.
Sales of this product surged in February 2003 after the US Department of Homeland Security advised families to stock it, along with plastic sheeting, for emergencies.
In 2024 a crypto entrepreneur paid $6.2 million at Sotheby's for Maurizio Cattelan's 'Comedian', an artwork made of a banana and this.
This silver-gray, cloth-backed roll that tears by hand is the classic quick fix for almost anything, and it helped Apollo 13's crew rig their carbon dioxide filters.

duct-tape.writerNotes: Clue 2: the Stoudt letter is widely reported (Wikipedia, trade press), but a search turned up no archival copy; the clue says only that she wrote proposing it, not that she invented it.

clues.text: This meme genre's name was a runner-up for the American Dialect Society's 'most creative' word of 2007, losing to 'Googlegänger'.
In 2007 a Lancaster University researcher based a joke programming language on this meme genre's captions; its programs open with 'HAI' and close with 'KTHXBYE'.
A 2016 taxidermy sculpture by Eva and Franco Mattes, based on this meme genre's figure who peeks through a hole in the ceiling, joined SFMOMA's collection in 2020.
These internet memes pair photos of kittens and other felines with captions in deliberately broken English, such as 'I can has cheezburger?'

lolcats.writerNotes: Clue 3: The Art Newspaper (May 2020) says the sculpture entered SFMOMA's permanent collection 'this year'; the ceiling-hole description of the character comes from Wikipedia.

clues.text: This group of stars is thought to be the small clump of gold dots on the Nebra sky disc, a Bronze Age disc dug up in Germany in 1999.
This cluster's dawn rising in late June or early July marks Matariki, the Māori new year, which has been a New Zealand public holiday since 2022.
clues.how: written, moved from clue 3 after review

clues.text: Galileo's 1610 book Sidereus Nuncius included a sketch of this cluster showing 36 stars, though only about half a dozen are easy to see with the naked eye.
clues.how: written, moved from clue 2 after review

clues.text: This star cluster in Taurus is named in Greek myth for the daughters of the Titan Atlas, and Subaru's six-star badge depicts it.

pleiades.writerNotes: Nebra disc: Wikipedia says the cluster of dots 'is thought to refer to the Pleiades', so clue 1 hedges. Its Bronze Age date was challenged in 2020 but later analyses confirmed it. Alias 'Seven Sisters' means the clues avoid the words 'seven' and 'sisters'.

clues.text: This painter's Nativity was cut from its frame in a Palermo oratory in 1969 and has never been found; the FBI put the theft on its Top Ten Art Crimes list.
In 1604 a tavern waiter sued this painter for throwing a plate of artichokes in his face.
This painter's only signed work, an altarpiece in Valletta, Malta, carries his name written in the blood spilling from John the Baptist's neck.
Born Michelangelo Merisi, this Italian master of dramatic light and shadow killed a man in a fight in Rome in 1606 and fled under a death sentence.

caravaggio.writerNotes: FBI listed the Nativity theft in its Top Ten Art Crimes in 2005 (Wikipedia); the FBI page itself returned 403. Clue 4 says 'a fight' because Wikipedia says it is unclear whether it was a brawl or a duel.

clues.text: This plant may mark the site of a long-abandoned building, because it thrives where human and animal waste have made the soil rich in phosphate and nitrogen.
In Hans Christian Andersen's 'The Wild Swans', a princess gathers this plant in graveyards and, under a vow of silence, knits it into shirts to free her 11 brothers.
At a yearly contest in a Dorset pub, entrants get one hour to strip and eat the raw leaves from as many two-foot stalks of this plant as they can.
This plant's hollow hairs work like tiny hypodermic needles that inject histamine into the skin, and folk wisdom says to rub the rash with a dock leaf.

stinging-nettle.writerNotes: Clue 1 hedges with 'may', as Wikipedia does. Skipped the WWI German uniform story because Wikipedia says there is little evidence for it. Dock-leaf remedy is framed as folk wisdom; Wikipedia says there is no evidence of a chemical effect.

clues.text: Around 1930, doctor Lucy Wills used this cheap spread to cure an anaemia of pregnancy in Bombay; the unknown nutrient behind the cure later proved to be folate.
In October 2016, a price row between Tesco and Unilever over the pound's fall after the Brexit vote saw this Unilever spread pulled from Tesco's website.
This spread was first made in 1902 in Burton upon Trent, from leftover yeast supplied by the Bass Brewery.
This sticky, salty British yeast-extract spread is named after the French cooking pot pictured on its label, and its 'Love it or hate it' ads began in 1996.

marmite.writerNotes: Lucy Wills: her Bombay work ran 1928-1933 and her yeast-extract paper came out in 1931, hence 'around 1930'. Wikipedia says Marmite was the cheapest yeast extract she could use. The 'Wills factor' was shown in the 1940s to be folate.

clues.text: This game sold poorly after its 1956 launch because its appeal was hard to get across in an ad, until its maker threw parties where people could play it.
The toy maker who launched this game, Edwin S. Lowe, had earlier turned a carnival game called Beano into a national pastime under a new name: Bingo.
The story goes that an anonymous Canadian couple invented this game as 'The Yacht Game' and traded the rights for 1,000 gift sets.
In this game, players get up to three rolls a turn to make scoring combinations with five dice, and five of a kind shares the game's name.

yahtzee.writerNotes: The Canadian couple story is Hasbro's and Lowe's own account, so clue 3 says 'the story goes'.

clues.text: This star pattern's Chinese name was given to China's satellite navigation system, BeiDou.
Five of this pattern's stars travel through space together, but the two at its ends drift the other way, so over many thousands of years its shape will warp.
A seventh-grader living in an Alaska orphanage won a 1927 contest with a flag that shows this star pattern in gold on a blue field.
This group of seven stars in Ursa Major has a four-star bowl and a three-star handle, and the two front stars of the bowl point to the North Star.

big-dipper.writerNotes: Clue 3: Benny Benson's age differs by source (13 per alaska.edu and the 1927 Legion report, 14 per Wikipedia), so the clue says 'seventh-grader' (alaska.edu). Clue 2: sources give the timescale as tens of thousands to 100,000 years, so the clue says 'many thousands of years'.

clues.text: This painting was listed in early Spanish royal records as 'Del Madroño', after the strawberry-tree fruit that features prominently in its center panel.
When this triptych is closed, its grey-green outer wings show the world as a globe, probably on the third day of Creation.
In 2014 a college student transcribed the music written on a sinner's buttocks in this painting's hell panel and posted a recording of it online.
Hieronymus Bosch painted this triptych, now in Madrid's Prado, whose panels run from Eden through a crowd of naked pleasure-seekers to a nightmarish hell.

garden-of-earthly-delights.writerNotes: Clue 1: Wikipedia says the 1593 Escorial record calls it 'Del Madroño' and Philip IV's inventory 'La Pintura del Madroño'; a 1605 description called it the 'strawberry painting' for the strawberry-tree fruit in the center panel. The Prado page returned 403 to WebFetch; its content (grisaille Third Day of Creation, provenance) was confirmed from search results.

clues.text: Kericho, a tea-growing town in Kenya's highlands, is reputed to hold the world record for the most days of this weather in a single year.
In the Middle Ages, Europeans rang church bells and fired cannons to ward this off, and some farmers still fire acetylene 'cannons' at storms, with no evidence they work.
In 2010 a piece of this that fell in Vivian, South Dakota, set US records at 8 inches across and almost 2 pounds.
These lumps of ice form in thunderstorm updrafts, and weather spotters describe their size by comparing them to peas, golf balls and softballs.

hail.writerNotes: Clue 1 is hedged ('reputed') because the record count differs by source (132 days, or 113 days in 1965) and rests on Wikipedia. Clue 3: 8.0 inches diameter and 1.9375 lb per NWS and the NCEC memo.

clues.text: Two food historians argue this dessert descends from the Spanische Windtorte, an Austro-Hungarian meringue cake, by way of tortes German immigrants made in America.
In 2005 New Zealand students made a 64-metre-long version of this from 5,000 egg whites, beating a 45-metre one made for Wellington's Te Papa museum.
This dessert is a Christmas Day favorite in the southern summer, more often topped with kiwifruit in New Zealand and with passionfruit in Australia.
This crisp-shelled, soft-centred meringue dessert is named after a Russian ballerina, and both Australia and New Zealand claim to have invented it.

pavlova.writerNotes: Clue 1 is the claim of Andrew Wood and Annabelle Utrecht (2015), not settled fact, so it says 'argue'. The eatyourbooks page returned 403 to WebFetch; its content was confirmed from search results. Clue 2 is pinned to 2005 because the record has since been beaten (Norway, then Finland).

clues.text: This 1984 video game lets a second player steer the flying targets with a regular controller, a feature many fans first learned of from Seth Rogen's tweets in 2018.
This game sold more than 28 million copies, mostly because it came packed in with the console rather than being bought on its own.
This game grew out of a 1976 electronic light-gun toy of the same name that Gunpei Yokoi and Masayuki Uemura designed for Nintendo.
clues.how: written, moved from clue 2 after review

clues.text: In this NES game you shoot at flying birds with the Zapper light gun, and a dog laughs at you whenever you miss.

duck-hunt.writerNotes: Clue 1: the NES manual says the control pad is used in Game A for the second player to control the duck's flight; Rogen tweeted about it on 17 September 2018. Clue 2 rests on Wikipedia and a Spanish copy of it.

clues.text: This astronaut's mother was born Marion Moon, and his MIT doctorate on orbital rendezvous led fellow astronauts to nickname him 'Dr. Rendezvous'.
A Presbyterian elder, this astronaut privately took communion with bread and wine from his church near Houston after landing on the Moon.
In 2002, at age 72, this astronaut punched a Moon-landing conspiracy theorist who confronted him at a Beverly Hills hotel, and police declined to press charges.
This Apollo 11 astronaut became the second person to walk on the Moon, stepping onto the surface about 19 minutes after Neil Armstrong.

buzz-aldrin.writerNotes: Aldrin is alive as of the latest news found (Artemis II crew wished him a happy 96th birthday, January 2026), so no clue uses the present tense about him or mentions his 2023 marriage (his wife Anca Faur died in October 2025).

clues.text: This painting was too big for a Boeing 747, so in 1999 it flew from Paris to Tokyo standing upright in a pressurized case aboard an Airbus Beluga.
The pistol-waving boy in this painting is widely believed to have inspired Gavroche in Victor Hugo's 'Les Misérables'.
Coldplay used this painting, with 'Viva La Vida' written across it in white, as the cover of their 2008 album.
Eugène Delacroix painted this tribute to the July Revolution of 1830, in which a bare-breasted woman in a Phrygian cap raises the French tricolour over a barricade.

liberty-leading-the-people.writerNotes: Clue 1: the 'too big for a 747' detail is from Wikipedia only; Airbus's own press release confirms the 1999 Paris-Tokyo Beluga flight but not the reason.

clues.text: This plant's flowers are often said to have sold in ancient Rome for 100 denarii a pound, but Pliny gave that price for the costlier spikenard.
This plant's English name is generally thought to come, via Old French, from the Latin verb meaning 'to wash', a nod to its use in baths.
The story goes that French chemist René-Maurice Gattefossé, credited with coining the word 'aromatherapy', found that this plant's oil healed his burns from a 1910 lab explosion.
This violet-flowered herb of the mint family is dried and tucked into sachets among stored clothes to scent them and keep moths away.

lavender.writerNotes: Clue 3 is hedged ('The story goes') because EBSCO says 'sources suggest' and that some historians doubt it was an accident; the 1910 date comes from the publisher's description of Gattefossé's book. Clue 2: Wikipedia hedges the etymology ('generally thought').

clues.text: One of this drink's common names is said to come from a nickname of Hong Kong actress Amy Yip, which was slang for a busty woman.
This drink's invention is claimed by rival cafés in Taichung and Tainan, but a 2019 court ruling found it could not be patented and credited neither.

clues.text: Shipping snarls on the US West Coast and the 2021 Suez Canal blockage left shops in the US and Canada short of this drink's key ingredient.
This sweet Taiwanese drink is famous for the chewy balls of tapioca starch that sit at the bottom of the cup.

bubble-tea.writerNotes: Aliases ban 'boba', 'pearl' and 'milk' as well as 'bubble' and 'tea', so no clue uses them. Clue 2: Wikipedia says the Amy Yip nickname was first adopted for the tapioca balls, and 'boba' then became a name for the drink.

clues.text: This game's first known mention is in a Chinese book from around 1600, which calls it 'shoushiling' and claims Han dynasty warlords played it.
In 2005 Christie's beat Sotheby's at this game, on an 11-year-old's advice, to win the right to sell a Japanese firm's art collection worth about $20 million.
Male side-blotched lizards come in three throat colors, and biologists compare the way their rival mating tactics balance out to this game.
In this hand game, a closed fist beats two fingers held in a V, the V beats a flat hand, and the flat hand covers the fist.

rock-paper-scissors.writerNotes: Clue 1 says the book 'claims' the Han dynasty origin because Wikipedia calls that claim ambiguous. Aliases ban 'stone', 'roshambo' and 'rochambeau', so no clue mentions the Comte de Rochambeau legend.

clues.text: This sport was the cover for a 1763 attack: Ojibwe warriors staged a game of it outside Fort Michilimackinac as a ruse to get in, then took the fort from the British.
This sport was an Olympic medal event only in 1904 and 1908, with Canadian teams winning both times, and it returns at Los Angeles 2028 in a format called sixes.
The Haudenosaunee, or Six Nations of the Iroquois, field their own national team in this sport, the only First Nations team sanctioned for international competition in any sport.
This sport, Canada's national summer sport since 1994, is played by catching and flinging a rubber ball with a mesh-pocketed stick, and its name is French for 'the stick'.

lacrosse.writerNotes: Clue 1: sources give June 2 or June 4, 1763 for the attack, so the clue gives only the year. Some accounts say the game was Ojibwe against Sauk; Wikipedia says the Ojibwe staged it.

clues.text: This children's show was filmed on a Warwickshire farm, where the hole left by its set was later flooded into a pond to deter trespassing fans.
This show's theme-song single reached No. 1 in the UK in December 1997, stayed in the top 75 for 32 weeks and sold over a million copies.
In 1999 Jerry Falwell's newspaper warned parents that one of this show's characters was a gay-pride symbol, because he is purple and has a triangle-shaped antenna.
This BBC preschool show, first aired in 1997, stars Tinky Winky, Dipsy, Laa-Laa and Po, four creatures named for the TV screens on their bellies.

teletubbies.writerNotes: Clue 1: sources disagree on when the site was flooded (Wikipedia and the Coventry Telegraph say 2013, the fan wiki says 2003), so the clue gives no year.

clues.text: This 1975 craze's inventor later tried other novelties such as 'Sand Breeding Kits', but none drew anything like the same interest.
This novelty's maker paid under a penny for what went in each box, sold it for $3.95, and moved nearly 1.5 million before the fad died after Christmas 1975.
In January 2023 the film studio A24 sold a $35 googly-eyed version of this 1970s fad, tied to 'Everything Everywhere All at Once', and it sold out within a day.
This 1975 craze from ad man Gary Dahl was a smooth Mexican beach stone sold in a cardboard carrier with air holes and straw, plus a care and training manual.

pet-rock.writerNotes: Sales are given as 'nearly 1.5 million' (Pet Rock article); the Gary Dahl article says 1.3 to 1.5 million.

clues.text: This sport gave boxer Eddie Eagan a 1932 Winter Olympic gold, making him, as of 2026, the only person with Summer and Winter golds in different sports.
This sport's oldest surviving track, opened at St. Moritz on New Year's Day 1904, is the only one still made of natural ice, rebuilt from snow each winter by about 15 workers.
Twice, in 1998 and 2018, two crews shared this sport's Olympic two-man gold after a dead heat, and a Canadian crew was one of them both times.
Jamaica's first team in this sport, at the 1988 Winter Olympics, inspired the 1993 Disney comedy 'Cool Runnings'.

bobsleigh.writerNotes: Clue 1: Gillis Grafström won figure-skating gold at both a Summer (1920) and Winter Games, which is why the clue says 'in different sports'. Clue 2: Wikipedia says the crew starts mid-November; FIL and Swissinfo say end of November. The clue avoids the start date.

clues.text: This 1984 film's makers tried using monkeys for its creatures, but dropped the idea when the test monkey panicked on being made to wear a creature's head.
In this film the heroine, Kate, explains that her father died climbing down the chimney dressed as Santa Claus, a speech studio executives wanted cut.

clues.text: Criticism of the PG ratings given to this film and 'Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom' led Steven Spielberg to propose a new PG-13 rating, introduced that same year.

clues.text: This 1984 horror-comedy turns on three rules for caring for a cute furry creature: keep it out of the light, never let it get wet, and never feed it after midnight.

gremlins.writerNotes: Clue 1 (the monkey test) is confirmed by Wikipedia only; the Mental Floss list does not mention it.

clues.text: This gymnast was spotted at age six turning cartwheels in a schoolyard with a friend, who grew up to become one of her country's top ballerinas.
A 1971 film tune, also the theme of The Young and the Restless, reached the US Top 10 renamed in this gymnast's honor, though she never performed to it.
In November 1989 this gymnast fled her country on foot at night, crossing into Hungary just weeks before the revolution that toppled Ceaușescu.
At the 1976 Montreal Olympics, this 14-year-old Romanian scored the first perfect 10 in Olympic gymnastics, which the scoreboard could only show as 1.00.

nadia-comaneci.writerNotes: Clue 2: the tune is 'Cotton's Dream' from Bless the Beasts and Children, renamed 'Nadia's Theme' after ABC's 1976 Olympics montage; it peaked at No. 8 on the Billboard Hot 100 in December 1976. Clue 3: sources disagree on the group size (6 or 7), so the clue leaves it out.

clues.text: In the Spanish dub of this sitcom, its hapless Spanish waiter was turned into an Italian from Naples called Paolo.
In 2000, a British Film Institute poll of TV industry professionals ranked this sitcom, which ran for just 12 episodes, first among the 100 greatest British TV programmes.
The Torquay hotel owner who inspired this sitcom's lead character is said to have thrown Eric Idle's briefcase out of a window in case it held a bomb.
John Cleese co-wrote this sitcom with Connie Booth and starred as Basil, a rude hotelier, in an episode remembered for the line 'Don't mention the war!'

fawlty-towers.writerNotes: Clue 3 is hedged ('is said to') because Donald Sinclair's widow said the stories were exaggerated, and accounts differ on briefcase vs bag; Wikipedia says briefcase and window.

clues.text: This toy began in the 1940s as a liquid-filled tube, inspired by a spirit-writing gadget that the inventor's mother, a Cincinnati clairvoyant, used with clients.
This toy got its present look in 1950, when Brunswick Billiards ordered it as a promotional item.
The 20-sided die floating inside this toy leans positive two to one, with 10 upbeat faces against 5 gloomy ones.
This black fortune-telling toy, now made by Mattel, gives replies such as 'Outlook not so good' when you shake it.

magic-8-ball.writerNotes: Clue 1: Mental Floss dates the liquid-filled tube (the Syco-Seer) to 1944; Wikipedia gives 1946 for the invention, so the clue says 'the 1940s'. Clue 2: CBS Sports dates it to 19 February 2015; asked if he wanted a trade, the toy said 'Very doubtful'.

clues.text: This quiz show was co-created by Steven Knight, who later created Peaky Blinders, and took its title from a Cole Porter song in the 1956 film High Society.
This show's tense music took its cue from a dissonant chord in 'Mars' from Holst's The Planets, and in later rounds its pitch rose a semitone with each question.
In 2003 a British Army major was convicted of cheating his way to this show's top prize, with a fellow contestant found to have coughed to signal answers.
Chris Tarrant in Britain and Regis Philbin in the US hosted this quiz show, where stuck contestants could 'Phone a Friend' or 'Ask the Audience.'

who-wants-to-be-a-millionaire.writerNotes: Clue 1: sources disagree on who picked the title (Wikipedia now says ITV's David Liddiment, a mirror says David Briggs), so the clue names no one. Clue 2: the semitone rise is from Wikipedia's British-show article only; Keith Strachan's article confirms the Holst chord. Clue 3: the Ingrams still deny cheating; the clue states the 2003 conviction.

clues.text: This decorative light's British inventor, a wartime reconnaissance pilot, also directed what is described as the first naturist film released publicly in the UK.

clues.text: This 1960s décor icon, first sold in Britain as the Astro, is a glass vessel in which blobs of wax, warmed by a bulb, rise and sink through liquid.

lava-lamp.writerNotes: Clue 1: the film is Travelling Light (1959), directed by Edward Craven Walker as Michael Keatering. Clue 3: Interesting Engineering says 100 lamps; Cloudflare's own blog says 'dozens', so the clue says 'about 100'.
